name: Fáŋ

catalog_citation: Mve, Jean Patrick. 2013. Aspects of the phonology of Fáŋ (draft version). MA thesis, Université de Yaoundé I. 171 pp. Open PDF: https://ubwp.buffalo.edu/kpaamcam/wp-content/uploads/sites/86/2024/09/Mve-2013-Fang.pdf (also https://www.acsu.buffalo.edu/~jcgood/Mve-2013-Fang.pdf)
catalog_locator: ch. IV-0 Introduction, printed p.83 = PDF p.102; sec. II 'The phonemic status of long vowels', printed pp.40-41 = PDF pp.56-57; also III-4-6/III-4-7 vowel lengthening/shortening pp.75-78 and the p.132 recommendation., text
catalog_quote: [p.83] Fáŋ happens to be a tone language like most African languages. The tone is a prosodic unit which has the same value as the phonemic consonants and vowels. [...] Moreover, unlike the stress, the tone is carried by a tone bearing unit (TBU), which can be any segment that can function as the peak of the syllable. Now, one should notice that only vowels are tone bearing units in Fáŋ for there is no syllabic nasals or syllabic laterals in the language in hand. [...] [pp.40-41] During our analysis, we have come to realized that the existing long vowels in this language appear solely in penultimate position which is not a relevant one for these sounds to be considered as distinctive phonemes. Thus, this seems to be a good reason to believe that long vowels are not underlying in Fáŋ. For Mutaka and Tamanji (2000: 38) state that, “allophonic length is sometimes manifested in penultimate position as in Swahioli, Chichewa, Kinande. Length is not contrastive in this position. This penultimate length is interpreted as the manifestation of stress in such languages.” Meanwhile, there are many other words in this language which do not have a penultimate long vowel. We will therefore have to consider these long vowels as marginalized phonemes, since their occurrences are very few in Fáŋ.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Fang is described as a tone language with three underlying level tones (L, M, H; surface super-high and contour tones derived). The description contains no rule for word stress or accent. The only prosodic-prominence-adjacent facts given are that (non-contrastive or marginal) vowel length surfaces only in penultimate position of the word (and is lost word-finally), which the author notes is the position where Bantu-type penultimate stress-lengthening occurs elsewhere, without asserting it for Fang; Good et al. 2011:148 independently note the root-initial vowel is sometimes noticeably longer.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress rule stated); author notes many words lack a penultimate long vowel
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms of isolated nouns and verbs (with class prefix / infinitive ə́-); no phrase-level prosody treated — author explicitly defers prosodic and metrical phonology to future work (p.132).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Fang [fak] of Fang village, Lower Fungom, Menchum Division, NW Region, Cameroon (Glottolog fang1248, Yemne-Kimbi). Good et al. 2011:146 explicitly distinguish it from Fang [fan] (Beti cluster, fang1246) — name overlap coincidental. Mve's consultants were Fang speakers resident in Fang, Wum and Yaoundé. Lovegren 2012 (stem-initial accent) concerns Mungbam (mung1266), a different Lower Fungom language, and must not be transferred to Fang.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 3.6 Fang (pp.146-152); 3.6.2 Phonology covers consonants, vowels and tones only. p.148: 'noticeable differences in vowel length in surface forms', root-initial vowel of tə̄wésə́ 'culverts' longer, length possibly contrastive; pp.148-149: at least three tone levels plus contours. No word on stress/accent for Fang (the only 'stress' token in the article is 'It should be stressed that..'). PDF itself is altcha-gated on Persée; the copy we hold is Persée's embedded per-page scanned text layer for pp.101-164.
